niches.name: Bodyweight training, explained by the research
niches.identity: research-checked answers to practical bodyweight-training questions (isometric holds, push-ups a day): what a small habit really does inside the body and when, and how to do it at home, with honest limits
niches.boundary: stops being this niche when the body is not being trained: diets and weight loss, injury or medical treatment, sports biography, or a follow-along workout with no science behind it
niches.viewer_reward: [I] the truth about a small training habit from someone who read the studies: what changes inside the body and when, something to try at home, and the underdog hope that the slim one wins

members.why: its card: fitness and bodyweight strength, exercise science explained; isometric holds train tendons, told with a self-test, the studies and a 12-week home plan
its card: fitness science, bodyweight training, exercise physiology; what 20 push-ups a day do to the body from the first rep to ten years, each stage a study with its caveat

formats.form: underdog-promise explainer: a self-test now, the research, a home routine, the result decoded at the end
evidence-led timeline of a daily habit (first rep to ten years), one study and one caveat per stage

comparable_cohorts.why_comparable: both answer one practical training question from the studies in a single sitting, 7.4 and 7.8 min (both under the long-form floor)

evidence.observed: the slim hero still hangs after the big guy drops, then wins the arm wrestle: the underdog promise comes before any science
the viewer does a half push-up hold now against an on-screen stopwatch and keeps the number; it is decoded at 06:24 on 'our own simple scale, not a medical test'
the week-four plateau is predicted before the viewer hits it: 'that's exactly when most people quit'
'your chest has opinions' over the mascot in bed reaching for coffee: personified biology and a dry joke at the point most people quit
'Here's the honest part though': fat and size unchanged at one month, 'anybody promising you a new chest in 30 days is selling something'
the famous 96% heart statistic is shown big, then 'I'd be lying to you if I left it there' and corrected

niches.name: The whole story of a famous company
niches.identity: a famous company's history from its founding to its empire, told fast as a chain of turning points (accidents, failures, blunders) that turned out to be the strategy; the promise of the complete history in a fixed number of minutes is itself part of what brings the audience back
niches.boundary: stops being this niche when the company is not the protagonist: a founder's biography, a product review, an industry or market explainer, or business advice without the company's story
niches.viewer_reward: [I] the surprise that a world-famous company nearly failed and was made by accidents, blunders and one insight; absurd true details and small hard numbers; the whole arc in one sitting

members.why: its card: business history, company origin stories, brands and marketing; Coca-Cola from a failed medicine to a world brand through a chain of accidents and turning points

its card: business history, company origin stories, space and technology; SpaceX from rejection and three failed launches to reusable rockets, the same complete-history-in-minutes series promise as V004

formats.form: chronological speedrun of lucky accidents and turning points, closed by a recap that names them
underdog company history: rejection, near-ruin, a last chance, escalating wins, a full-circle callback

comparable_cohorts.why_comparable: the same series promise and telling (a whole company history in a stated number of minutes), 8.9 and 11.0 min, both long-form

evidence.observed: four contrasting facts in 17 s (two billion servings a day, a failed medicine, money lost in year one, one of the best-known brands), then the title line
the 'greatest business mistake' is announced with a trophy 30 s before it happens, then reversed: the $1 bottling rights 'accidentally created a genius system'
'What they forgot to test was what the Old Coke meant to people.' over endless taste-test tables, then a protest crowd
the spreadsheet on the flight home: 'the problem wasn't physics, it was price', the insight every later turn serves
three failed launches, each with a year and a cause (a corroded nut), both companies short of cash, then 'Last chance. And it worked.'
'Remember where this story started?' over a humiliation / vindication diptych: the opening rejection paid off as a full circle

niches.name: How people survive the desert's heat and drought
niches.identity: how people live where heat and missing water should make life impossible (50-degree days, no rivers): the counterintuitive physics and engineering behind it, explained step by step until the paradox makes sense
niches.boundary: stops being this niche when the desert or the heat is only a setting (travel, war, wildlife, a culture's history for its own sake), or when the story is about money, politics or markets rather than how people get through the climate
niches.viewer_reward: [I] a paradox of desert life (thick walls, more clothes, water with no rivers) made to make sense step by step, the pleasure of a wrong intuition corrected, and admiration or alarm at what it takes

members.why: its card: everyday science, architecture and engineering; how homes stayed cool in 50-degree heat without machines, passive cooling as a system (ancient Egypt is the setting, the cooling is the subject)
its card: everyday science, culture and survival, human body; why desert peoples wear more clothes in extreme heat, the robe as a wearable cooling system and the viewer's instinct corrected

its card: geography and infrastructure, water and resources; how a desert country with no rivers gets its water belongs here, but its subject is also oil-wealth economics and a fragile national infrastructure, a geography explainer's territory

formats.form: problem-solution chain: each fix creates the next problem
paradox explainer with a second paradox held back for the last third

comparable_cohorts.why_comparable: both a second-person teacher's explainer that voices the viewer's doubt and corrects it with heat physics, step by step, in one long-form sitting, 9.2 and 10.2 min; V010 (9.5 min) is left out for its telling, a third-person documentary read at 145 wpm over a music bed, not for its runtime

evidence.observed: 'You wake up, and the air is already trying to kill you': second-person peril, then people sitting cool inside thick walls and a one-word 'How?' at 01:05
the viewer's objection is voiced ('It seems like it should make things worse'), then 'Here's the part almost no one expects': the wall delays the heat until after dark
'Problem solved, right?' 'Not quite': the sealed box traps air, and that side effect opens the next section
'Your instinct screams that this is insane': the viewer's own intuition is set up as what the video will correct
'That air is no longer cooling you. It's cooking you.': the paradox dissolves because a hidden premise changes
a second paradox held back (black absorbs heat, yet Bedouins wear black), answered by an experiment's null result and the bellows effect taught earlier
after oil gushes with cash, 'But there is a slight problem. You cannot drink crude oil.', then a dry riverbed: the paradox as a joke
the wheat miracle is shown at full glory, then 'completely backfired': mud from a pipe in a cave, a rusted pivot over dead stalks

niches.name: Money decisions after 60, with the real math
niches.identity: money decisions people face around retirement (here renting vs buying a home after 60), worked out with real numbers over the years that follow and with the factors specific to older viewers: a fixed income, aging in place, flexibility
niches.boundary: stops being this niche when the viewer is not at or near retirement (general investing, a first home, budgeting for young people), or when it becomes market news or product selling rather than one decision worked out
niches.viewer_reward: [I] a fair, numbers-first answer to a decision the viewer faces now, a race with a running score to follow, and a twist that hands the outcome back to the viewer's own behaviour

members.why: its card: personal finance, retirement planning, housing; renting vs buying after 60, two matched retirees followed for 20 years and then stress-tested, built around a fixed income and aging in place

formats.form: two-character head-to-head simulation with checkpoints, then a stress test that flips the verdict

evidence.observed: the two retirees are made identical item by item (age 62, the same street, $400,000 each, the same Social Security check) before one choice splits them
'the first number that should make every retiree sit up': rent of $2,015 eats almost the whole average Social Security check, drawn as a house biting a cheque
'They are basically tied' at year 5, then the question is turned to the viewer: 'Not would I like to. Am I actually going to?'
Bill's $30,000 aging-in-place remodel against Margaret moving on one month's notice: 'flexibility is... a health plan'
'Case closed? Not so fast': if Bill spends the difference, Margaret wins by almost half a million

outliers.why: its card: prehistory and human origins, animals and evolution, human-animal relationships; how wolves became dogs, from fear to love. No other reference shares that audience (dog lovers, animal-evolution and human-origins viewers), and one broad-curiosity video does not settle which of them it serves. It still teaches craft: the fear-to-love arc set in the first minute, the 'this sounds fake' experiment as proof (02:20), the word ladder performed by the edit (06:10)

notes: Placed by subject, the audience's reason to come; looks, formats and voices shared across groups are in shared_across_niches. The cards' cohort_id labels were not used: cohorts here were decided with every reference in view. V013 and V035 share a setting (the deep human past), not a subject (cooling physics vs the dog's origin), so no ancient-life niche was made. V010 differs from V013 and V020 in look (moving AI clips), voice (145 wpm and a showman's register, against 178 and 213 wpm) and mood (irony and alarm rather than admiration); those do not split an audience, but its subject reaches into oil economics and national infrastructure, hence overlap. A first desert cohort of all three (V010, V013, V020: Standard 575 s) was replaced by the two core members: V010's runtime compares, its telling does not (third person, 145 wpm against 178 and 213). N4 rests on one reference whose audience is defined by life stage; it has no comparable cohort, so its length would be the user's own. V035 could stand as a niche of its own (animal origins, the human-animal bond) if the user wants that direction. Both N1 references are under the long-form floor.
